nodes.question: What recent changes have been made to forestry and land use policies in the State?
nodes.answer: The State has recently defined ambitions for forestry and land use, indicating more formal direction setting and greater prioritization of land use topics.
nodes.paragraph: Agriculture and land use policy creation in the State has historically been diffuse, with programs largely influenced by the direction of external donors. This has made it diffi- cult for central coordination and tracking of progress. The State has recently defined ambitions for forestry and land use, signaling the emergence of more for - mal direction setting and greater prioritization of land use topics. However, it notes that there is a signifi- cant need to bridge the gap between agricultural and forestry agendas (Ekiti State Forestry Commission 2021a). Spatial mapping and understanding of land use across Nigeria have been extremely limited, with only a handful of academic studies (e.g., Olorunfemi et al. 2020; Fasona et al. 2020; Abbas et al. 2018; Akiny - emi 2013; Koranteng et al. 2016), and two national land cover surveys conducted since 1976 (Fasona et al. 2020). nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Deforestation prevention|Forest conservation policies_qna_001
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What are some of the priorities emphasized by the EU forest-related policy instruments?
nodes.answer: The priorities include renewable energy, nature protection, biodiversity conservation, and climate and land use policies.
nodes.paragraph: Consequently, a patchwork of EU forest-related policy instruments developed, each emphasizing its own priorities (e.g., renewable energy, nature protection, biodiversity conservation, and climate and land use policies) and preferred governance mechanism (such as state regulation, e.g. binding law, market-related governance, e.g. payment for ecosystem services, or community initiatives, e.g. awareness raising and capacity build- ing). This patchwork is prone to conflicts between policies, and forest policy coordina- tion and integration at the EU level has subsequently been described as weak (Aggestam & Giurca, 2021; P Izl et al., 2018; Wolfslehner et al., 2020). Addressing these challenges within the EU multi-level governance framework trig- gers polarized discussions. The increased issuance of policy instruments by the Euro- pean Commission, especially since the Green Deal, signals a growing interest in advancing EU forest policy (Aggestam & Giurca, 2021). Simultaneously, a political debate evolves around the legitimacy of the EU S legal competence on forests (Lazdinis et al., 2019; see also Onida, 2020), with some member states opposing EU competency as conflicting with their national interests (Wolfslehner et al., 2020).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Deforestation prevention|Forest conservation policies_qna_003
nodes.label: Research Questions
nodes.question: What are the two main research questions addressed in the exploration of EU forest policy?
nodes.answer: The two main research questions are: 1) How do EU forest policy actors envisage forests and their ecosystem services in terms of perceived problems, preferred solutions, and responsibilities to govern forests? 2) How can Cultural Theory contribute to understanding overlaps and differences in these views, and what theoretical implications could arise from a better understanding of them?
nodes.paragraph: Political cultures point to the importance of mean- ing (Mamadouh, 1999b, p. 477). Cultural Theory (CT) is a long-established approach for such analyses (Thompson et al., 1990). CT, originating from the works of Douglas (1978) and Douglas and Wildavsky (1982) and developed by Thompson et al. (1990), analyzes how actors perceive the world (related risks, problems, solutions, etc.) and interact with their surroundings based on their values and beliefs (Chuang et al., 2020; Tansey, 2004). We set out to explore how CT could assist in understanding the roots of different perceptions in EU forest policy, investigating two main research questions: 1. How do EU forest policy actors envisage forests and their ecosystem services in terms of perceived problems, preferred solutions, and responsibilities to govern forests? Policy Sciences 2. How can Cultural Theory contribute to understanding overlaps and differences in these views and which theoretical implications could a better understanding of these over - laps and differences offer? Theoretical framework: cultural theory Cultural Theory identifies four main politically relevant worldviews: egalitarianism, indi- vidualism, hierarchy, and fatalism.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Deforestation prevention|Forest conservation policies_qna_004
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What impact did the policy change have on the classification of forested areas in Tasmania?
nodes.answer: The policy change led to high conservation value reserves being reclassified as production forestry land and previously used forestry land being converted into reserves.
nodes.paragraph: Data on forest quality are not captured by satellite imagery of tree cover extent, but these data can be aggregated with thematic maps for further inference. The swift parrot S breeding range exemplifies this challenge, as Tasmania has 72 76% vegetation cover42, but only a third of Tasmanian forests remaining are intact43 or of high integrity13,25. Within swift parrot important breeding areas (SPIBAs), forests with high integrity are even scarcer (4.2% VS. 29.4% statewide)25. Forest accounting (i.e. systematic measurement and tracking of forest condition and changes over time) in swift parrot habitat is complicated by shifts in land-use classification in forested areas following a policy change enacted a decade ago through the Forestry (Rebuilding the Forest Industry) Act 201444. This policy S purpose was to provide for the invigoration of the forest industry and for related purposes , thereby repealing prior legislation that sought to protect forests of high conservation value (i.e. the Tasmanian Forests Agreement Act 2013 ). Subsequently, high conservation value reserves were reclassified as production forestry land and previously used forestry land was converted into reserves21.
